                                                      PROJECT NO. 58481

                RULEMAKING TO IMPLEMENT                       §   PUBLIC UTILITY COMMISSION
              LARGE LOAD INTERCONNECTION                      §
              STANDARDS UNDER PURA § 37.0561                  §                   OF TEXAS



                                            HUNT ENERGY NETWORK, L.L.C.
                                             COMMENTS ON LARGE LOAD
                                           INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS


            Hunt Energy Network, L.L.C. (“HEN”) respectfully submits these comments in response to the
            Public Utility Commission of Texas (“Commission” or “PUC”) Staff’s proposed rulemaking in
            Project No. 58481 implementing large load interconnection standards under PURA § 37.0561.

                                                  INTRODUCTION AND COMMENTS

            Texas is sitting at an important crossroads. Large datacenter and other loads are seeking to build
            significant infrastructure in Texas which can strengthen the Texas economy and are important for
            national security, but that could place stress on our electric grid in ways we have not experienced
            before. The Texas Legislature recognized in PURA § 37.0561 that we must balance the desire to
            welcome these new industries, supporting business development, while also maintaining reliability
            and avoiding stranded transmission investment. While some of these new large loads are seeking
            interconnection to the ERCOT grid to fully support their demand, many are not. Increasingly,
            datacenter loads are developing prime power, on-site generation and energy storage solutions to
            serve all or a substantial portion of their demand (these are the so-called “Bring Your Own
            Generation (BYOG) Loads.”

                     In HEN’s experience working with these customers, they are pursuing these options
            because they need power faster than the grid can provide.       Because they are pursuing on-site
            generation solutions prior to grid interconnection, they often must overbuild generation capacity
            to ensure their required reliability. This means that these combined load and generation sites could
            be valuable resources for the ERCOT grid, and potentially a key component to solving ERCOT’s
            resource adequacy challenges and need for dispatchable generation. These are not only flexible
            loads that can shift between grid power and on-site generation, but they are also resources that can
 Docusign Envelope ID: 977AC677-B11B-4BC3-B9B8-DCFC06265442




            export excess generation onto the grid in critical times. They are future wholesale market
            participants with dispatchable generation.

                     BYOG Loads with paralleled, on-site generation that can serve as resources for the grid
            should be encouraged, and certainly not dis-incentivized, to interconnect. However, the Proposed
            Rule as drafted does not recognize or account for BYOG Loads, and the proposed fee structure
            could disincentivize these loads from interconnecting at all. This is because the fees and financial
            security required are based upon the maximum demand at the customer site, not the maximum
            demand for which the customer seeks power from the grid. As set forth further below, HEN
            proposes that the Commission recognize in the proposed rule that a large load may choose to self-
            limit the maximum demand that it will place onto the grid, consistent with Protocols that will be
            developed in the ERCOT process.

                     HEN appreciates that much of ERCOT’s and the Commission’s attention has been focused
            on the Batch Zero loads that are seeking to serve all of their demand from the grid, but the Proposed
            Rule is not limited to Batch Zero loads; rather, it is drafted to apply to all loads greater than 75
            MW that seek interconnection now or in the future. Therefore, HEN respectfully urges the
            Commission to specifically address the different nature of BYOG Loads in the Proposed Rule so
            that these loads have a reasonable path to grid interconnection in a way that supports and enhances
            reliability. To ignore these BYOG Loads now risks a future in which they remain islanded, with
            substantial generation infrastructure that could help solve the ERCOT’s future demand needs if
            they were interconnected.

                                                      RECCOMENDATIONS

            I. Financial Security

            HEN recommends that financial security requirements for large loads co-located with
            dispatchable generation be based on expected net grid usage during system peak conditions,
            rather than gross on-site peak demand. Financial obligations should reflect actual system
            reliance, not theoretical maximum demand.

            Accordingly, large load customers that are expected to be net-zero or net exporters during peak
            conditions should not be required to post financial security as though they are grid-dependent.



                                                             2
 Docusign Envelope ID: 977AC677-B11B-4BC3-B9B8-DCFC06265442




            Commission should calculate financial security obligations for BYOG configurations using
            existing net capacity contributions methodologies, such as those applied to Private Use
            Networks. This approach ensures that any requirement accurately reflects the large load’s peak-
            period reliance on the ERCOT system.

            II. Interconnection Fees

            HEN recommends that interconnection fees be assessed consistently with financial security
            requirements and based on expected maximum net import from the ERCOT grid during peak
            conditions for large loads co-located with dispatchable generation.

            Consistent treatment across provisions is critical to avoid over-allocation of costs and to maintain
            coherent price signals for efficient investment.

            III. Cost Allocation and Avoidance of Duplicative Recovery

            HEN is concerned that, as drafted, the rule risks stacking multiple cost recovery mechanisms on
            the same MWs of demand, including:

                 •   Financial security

                 •   Interconnection fees

                 •   Contributions in Aid of Construction (CIAC)

                 •   Potential ongoing transmission-related charges

            Without clear guardrails, these mechanisms may result in duplicative cost recovery and over-
            collection from projects that are not materially relying on the transmission system.

            HEN recommends that the Commission clarify that all financial obligations must be reasonably
            aligned with expected system use and structured to avoid duplicative recovery for the same MW
            of demand.

            IV. Treatment of BYOG Configurations

            HEN supports a framework that encourages large load customers to internalize reliability
            through the development of on-site, dispatchable generation.



                                                               3
 Docusign Envelope ID: 977AC677-B11B-4BC3-B9B8-DCFC06265442




            Where such configurations reduce or eliminate net demand during system peak conditions, those
            customers should not be treated or charged as grid-dependent loads.

            A rule that fails to account for net system impact risks discouraging private investment that:

                 •   Reduces peak demand

                 •   Enhances system reliability

                 •   Provides potential system benefits

            V. Minimum Demand and Take-or-Pay Constructs

            Any minimum demand or take-or-pay construct should be narrowly tailored to reflect actual
            reserved system capacity and applied only where necessary. Broad application risks creating a
            “pay-for-readiness” model that requires large load customers to pay for transmission capacity
            regardless of actual usage discouraging private investment and distorting efficient market
            outcomes.

            This approach is particularly inappropriate for BYOG configurations that materially reduce or
            eliminate peak demand, as it may:

                 •   Result in double payment for reliability
                 •   Distort investment signals
                 •   Deter capital formation in dispatchable generation



                                                             CONCLUSION

            HEN supports disciplined interconnection standards but emphasizes that all financial obligations
            must be grounded in cost causation and actual system use. Large loads that bring their own
            resources should not be charged as though their demand is being supplied by the ERCOT grid.

            HEN appreciates the opportunity to offer these comments and is available to answer questions the
            Commission may have.

               INTERCONNECTION STANDARDS                      §                 OF TEXAS
                   UNDER PURA § 37.0561                       §


                                         HUNT ENERGY NETWORK, L.L.C.
                                       EXECUTIVE SUMMARY OF COMMENTS

    Hunt Energy Network (HEN) supports the Commission’s effort in Project No. 58481 to bring discipline and
    transparency to the large load interconnection process. However, the proposed framework must be calibrated to
    reflect actual system reliance – not gross nameplate demand, to avoid discouraging private investment in on-
    site, dispatchable generation and to ensure fair competition.

    As drafted, the rule risks overburdening projects – particularly those deploying Bring Your Own Generation
    (BYOG) by treating them as grid-dependent even when they materially reduce or eliminate peak demand. This
    approach could unintentionally favor only the largest, most capitalized developers while discouraging private
    investment that enhances reliability.

    HEN recommends that:

        •   Financial security and interconnection fees be based on net grid usage during peak conditions.
        •   The Commission establish guardrails to prevent duplicative cost recovery across multiple mechanisms.
        •   BYOG configurations be appropriately recognized for reducing system burden and improving reliability.
        •   Any minimum demand or “take-or-pay” constructs be narrowly tailored to actual reserved capacity.

    Properly aligned, these rules can both protect the ERCOT system and unlock competitive, reliability-enhancing
    investment. Misaligned, they risk creating a “pay-for-readiness” regime that distorts price signals and
    suppresses innovation.
